blocks.text: A whole family of interview questions asks the same thing in different clothes: **for every element, find the nearest element to its left (or right) that is smaller (or bigger)**. Next Greater Element, Largest Rectangle in Histogram and Trapping Rain Water are all members. One technique solves them all in O(n): the **monotonic stack** — a stack whose items are always kept in sorted order.
We'll use one member of the family: **previous smaller element**. For each number, find the closest number **to its left** that is **smaller**, or -1 if there is none.

blocks.code:
nums = [4, 5, 2, 10, 8]
ans  = [-1, 4, -1, 2, 2]

5's previous smaller is 4.  2 has nothing smaller to its left: -1.
10's is 2.  8's is 2 (10 is closer, but not smaller).

blocks.alt: Bars for 4, 5, 2, 10 and 8, each labelled with its answer: 4 has none (-1), 5's is 4, 2 has none (-1), 10's is 2, and 8's is also 2 because 10 is closer but taller.

blocks.text: 1. Brute force: look left, one by one
For each index, walk left until you find something smaller. Simple, but in the worst case every element looks at every element before it.
**Time O(n²).** For `[1, 2, 3, …]` every answer is found in one step, but for `[5, 6, 7, …, 1, 2]`-style inputs the scans get long.
The insight: some numbers can never be an answer again
Look at `[4, 5, 2, …]`. Once **2** has arrived, can **4** or **5** ever be the previous smaller element of anything further right?

No. For any later number `x`, 2 is **closer** than 4 and 5, and it is **no bigger**. If 4 is smaller than `x`, then 2 is too — and 2 is found first. So 4 and 5 are **hidden behind** 2 forever. We can throw them away.

blocks.alt: Two moments. Before 2 arrives, the candidates are 4 and 5. When 2 arrives, 5 and 4 are popped because 2 is closer and smaller, leaving only 2 as a candidate.

blocks.text: Keep the surviving candidates on a stack. Because every bigger-or-equal number gets popped when a smaller one arrives, the stack is always **increasing from bottom to top** — that's what **monotonic** means. And the answer for the new number is simply whatever is left on **top** after popping.

items: **Pop** every candidate that is ≥ the current number — they're hidden from now on.
The **top** of the stack (if any) is the current number's previous smaller element.
**Push** the current number: it is a candidate for everything to its right.

blocks.caption: Watch the stack stay increasing, and count the pushes and pops.

blocks.text: Why it's O(n) even with a loop inside a loop

The inner `while` looks scary, but count what actually happens to each number: it is **pushed exactly once**, and it can be **popped at most once** — once it's gone, it never comes back. So across the whole run there are at most n pushes and n pops: **2n operations, O(n) time**. This counting trick is called **amortized analysis**.

blocks.alt: Each of the n numbers is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work is at most 2n stack operations, however the pops are spread out.

elements.text:
n pushes
+ at most n pops
= at most 2n steps  ->  O(n)

blocks.text: Flip the comparison and the scan direction and the same pattern answers all four questions:

blocks.alt: A table of the four variations. Previous smaller: scan left to right, pop while top is greater or equal, stack increasing. Previous greater: scan left to right, pop while top is smaller or equal, stack decreasing. Next smaller: scan right to left, pop while top is greater or equal, stack increasing. Next greater: scan right to left, pop while top is smaller or equal, stack decreasing.

elements.text:
question           scan            pop while top is    stack is

previous smaller   left -> right   >= current          increasing
previous greater   left -> right   <= current          decreasing
next smaller       right -> left   >= current          increasing
next greater       right -> left   <= current          decreasing

blocks.text: There's also a second way to get the **next** greater or smaller: scan **left to right** and fill in answers for the items you **pop** — the incoming number is the answer for everything it pops. You'll see both styles in **Next Greater Element I**.

items: **Next Greater Element I & II** — the nearest bigger number to the right (II wraps around).
**Largest Rectangle in Histogram** — each bar extends until the nearest shorter bar on both sides.
**Trapping Rain Water** — water fills between a bar and the nearest taller walls.
Also: Daily Temperatures, Online Stock Span, Sum of Subarray Minimums, Remove K Digits.
"Nearest smaller/greater to the left/right" is the **monotonic stack** pattern.
When a new element arrives, pop everything it **hides** — those elements can never be an answer again.
The stack stays **sorted**, and its top is the answer.
Each element is pushed once and popped at most once: **O(n)** instead of O(n²).
